Hanoi Old Quarter Guide (2026): Map, Things to Do, Night Market & Where to Stay
Hanoi Old Quarter
Hanoi Old Quarter Guide (2026): Map, Things to Do, Night Market & Where to Stay
A local's guide to Hanoi's Old Quarter: a simple map, 10 things to do, a one-day plan, the weekend night market, where to stay and how to get there from the airport.
Hanoi's Old Quarter is the tight grid of streets just north of Hoan Kiem Lake. For centuries it was the city's merchant district, and it is still where most visitors sleep, eat and spend their first day. The first hour can feel like a lot: motorbikes, shopfronts spilling onto the pavement, smells of grilled pork and incense. Give it a morning and it turns into one of the most walkable neighborhoods in Asia.
This guide is written by Hanoi locals. It covers how the quarter is laid out, the things actually worth your time, a simple one-day plan, the weekend night market, where to stay, how to get here from the airport, and where to take the best photos.
Morning in the Old Quarter: a flower seller on her daily round.
Hanoi Old Quarter at a glance
Quick facts
Where
Hoan Kiem district, between Hoan Kiem Lake (south) and Dong Xuan Market (north)
Size
About 15 minutes' walk from the lake to Dong Xuan Market without stops
Best for
Street food, walking, small temples, shopping, people-watching
Best time of day
Early morning (quiet streets, soft light) and early evening (food stalls open)
Weekend extra
Walking street and night market, Friday to Sunday evenings
How long
One full day for the highlights, two to slow down
A simple mental map of the Old Quarter
Think of the Old Quarter as a rough triangle:
South:
Hoan Kiem Lake. The easiest landmark, and where most walks begin.
North:
Dong Xuan Market, the big covered market at the top of Hang Dao and Hang Ngang.
East:
the Long Bien Bridge approach and the dyke road along the Red River. O Quan Chuong, the old city gate, sits on this side.
West:
Phung Hung street and its brick railway arches.
Many streets still carry the name of the trade once practiced there.
Hang
means "goods": Hang Bac was silver, Hang Ma paper offerings, Hang Thiec tin, Hang Buom sails. A few streets still sell what their name promises, which is half the fun of walking here. Locals call the area "36 streets", although there are more than that today.
Map tip:
Save a few pins before you go: your hotel, Hoan Kiem Lake, Dong Xuan Market, St. Joseph's Cathedral and O Quan Chuong gate. Street names change at almost every corner, so an app with offline maps is more useful than a paper map. If you lose your bearings, walk until you reach the lake and start again.
10 best things to do in the Hanoi Old Quarter
1. Walk around Hoan Kiem Lake at sunrise
From first light, locals jog, dance and practice tai chi around the lake. Cross the red The Huc Bridge to Ngoc Son Temple before the tour groups arrive. Read more about
Ngoc Son Temple
.
2. Step inside a merchant's tube house at 87 Ma May
Old Quarter houses are narrow at the front and run deep into the block, with small courtyards to let in light and air. The restored heritage house at 87 Ma May shows how a merchant family lived and traded under one roof. Entry costs around 20,000 VND; check the current fee at the door.
3. Visit Bach Ma Temple
At 76 Hang Buom, Bach Ma ("White Horse") Temple is one of the oldest temples in the quarter. Legend says a white horse showed the king where to build the city walls. It is free to enter and usually opens in the morning and mid-afternoon, with a break at lunch. Dress modestly.
4. Find O Quan Chuong, the last old city gate
Thang Long once had several gates. O Quan Chuong, first built in 1749 and rebuilt in the early 1800s, is the only one still standing. Motorbikes still pass through it, which makes it a great spot to watch the city move.
5. Get lost in the small lanes
The main streets are busy, but narrow alleys open into courtyards, family shrines and tiny cafés. Start with our
5 Old Quarter alleys to slow down in
.
6. Drink egg coffee where it was invented
Egg coffee is a Hanoi original, whipped egg yolk and sugar over strong coffee. Read the story of
Café Giảng and how to photograph it
.
7. Explore Dong Xuan Market and Hang Ma street
Dong Xuan is the city's largest covered market and sells mostly wholesale goods: fabric, household items, dried foods. The food stalls around its edges are the real draw. Nearby, Hang Ma glows with paper lanterns and offerings, especially in the weeks before Mid-Autumn Festival and Lunar New Year.
8. See St. Joseph's Cathedral
The neo-Gothic
St. Joseph's Cathedral
stands on the quarter's southwest edge, with cafés and lemon-tea stalls on the steps around it.
9. Spend an evening on Ta Hien
Ta Hien and the streets around it fill with low plastic stools, cold beer and music after dark. Our guide:
Ta Hien street, where Hanoi nights come alive
.
10. Walk out to the railway and Long Bien Bridge
Hanoi's railway history runs along the quarter's edges. Read our
Train Street safety guide
before you go, and consider the calmer view from Long Bien Bridge at sunset.
The Huc Bridge and Ngoc Son Temple, best visited early before the tour groups.
One perfect day in the Old Quarter
Morning
6:00–7:30: Hoan Kiem Lake and The Huc Bridge while the city exercises.
7:30: Breakfast phở or bánh cuốn at a small shop with stools on the pavement.
8:30–11:00: 87 Ma May, Bach Ma Temple and the lanes around Hang Buom and Ma May.
Afternoon
Lunch: bún chả. See our
bún chả guide
.
Egg coffee break, then Dong Xuan Market and Hang Ma.
Late afternoon: O Quan Chuong gate, then walk toward Long Bien Bridge for sunset.
Evening
Chả cá on its own street, or street food around Dong Xuan.
Friday to Sunday: the walking street and night market. Any night: a beer on Ta Hien.
Want a slower version across two days? Try our
calm 48-hour Hanoi itinerary
.
Hanoi Old Quarter night market and walking street
From Friday evening to Sunday night, the streets around Hoan Kiem Lake close to traffic and become a walking street, with families, street games and live music.
Inside the Old Quarter, the weekend night market runs along Hang Dao, Hang Ngang and Hang Duong, heading north toward Dong Xuan Market. Expect clothing, souvenirs, snacks and crowds.
When:
Friday to Sunday, from around 7 pm until about midnight. Times can shift, so check with your hotel on the day.
Tips:
Go early in the evening before it gets packed. Keep your phone in a front pocket, and bargain politely at clothing stalls.
Where to eat in the Old Quarter
The Old Quarter is one of the best places in Vietnam to eat well on a small budget. Start with:
Bún chả:
grilled pork with noodles and herbs.
Our bún chả guide
.
Chả cá Lã Vọng:
turmeric fish with dill, a dish with its own street.
Origins and how to eat it
.
Bánh mì, phở and more:
see our
honest Hanoi street food guide
.
A simple rule: if a stall is full of locals and has one dish on the sign, order that dish.
Hanoi Old Quarter photos: where and when to shoot
Yellow facades, green shutters, tangled power lines, lanterns and shopfronts make the Old Quarter Hanoi's most photogenic neighborhood.
Early morning
for empty streets and soft light around the lake.
Late afternoon
for warm light on Hang Ma lanterns and the old gate.
Blue hour
for shop lights and motorbike trails, shot from the pavement or a café upstairs.
For exact spots and timing, see our
15 best photo spots in Hanoi
. Before you photograph people or shops, read our
Hanoi photography etiquette guide
.
Want photos of yourself in these streets, not just of the streets? See how a portrait looks around Dong Xuan in our
story of Thin with Harry
, or book a
private Hanoi photoshoot
with a local photographer-guide.
Thin outside Dong Xuan Market, photographed by Harry. The market sign keeps the Old Quarter in the frame.
Where to stay in or near the Old Quarter
Staying inside or on the edge of the Old Quarter puts you within walking distance of the lake, the food and the night market. Pick your area by how much noise you can live with.

Light sleepers should ask for a room away from the street. Curious about the French Quarter after dark? Our
Hanoi night photoshoot story
was shot around Trang Tien.
How to get from Hanoi airport to the Old Quarter
Noi Bai International Airport is roughly 30 km north of the Old Quarter. Allow 45–60 minutes by car, more at rush hour.
Ride-hailing (Grab, Xanh SM):
the simplest door-to-door option. Check the fare in the app before you confirm.
Airport bus 86:
leaves from outside the arrivals area and runs to Hanoi Railway Station, passing near the Old Quarter and Hoan Kiem Lake. It has a flat fare of about 45,000 VND and runs roughly every 30 minutes from early morning to around 10 pm. Check the current timetable before you fly.
City bus 17:
the cheapest option, to Long Bien bus station on the Old Quarter's edge. It is slower and makes more stops.
Hotel transfer:
many Old Quarter hotels arrange pickup. Confirm the price in writing.
Practical tips
Crossing the street:
walk at a steady pace and don't stop suddenly. Our
guide to crossing the street in Hanoi
explains how.
Pavements are parking lots.
Expect to walk in the road at times. Keep to the edge.
Dress for temples:
cover shoulders and knees for Ngoc Son, Bach Ma and other temples.
Cash helps:
many small food stalls prefer cash. Carry small notes.
Plan the bigger trip:

Frequently asked questions
How many days do you need in the Hanoi Old Quarter?
One full day covers the highlights. Two days let you slow down, add the French Quarter and enjoy more evenings.
Is the Hanoi Old Quarter safe?
It is generally safe for visitors, including solo travelers. The main risks are traffic and petty theft in crowds. Watch your phone and bag at night markets.
What is the best time of day to explore the Old Quarter?
Early morning, for quiet streets and soft light around the lake, and early evening, when the food stalls open.
Is the Old Quarter walkable?
Yes. Hoan Kiem Lake to Dong Xuan Market is about a 15-minute walk without stops, and most sights in this guide are within 20 minutes of each other on foot.
When is the Hanoi Old Quarter night market open?
Friday to Sunday evenings, from around 7 pm until about midnight, on Hang Dao, Hang Ngang and Hang Duong.
Is it better to stay in the Old Quarter or the French Quarter?
Stay in the Old Quarter for food and atmosphere on your doorstep. Choose the French Quarter if you want quieter nights and are happy to walk 10–15 minutes in.

The best way to see the quarter is on foot with someone who knows which alley leads to which courtyard. Our local hosts can turn your walk into photos you will keep.

15 Best Photo Spots in Hanoi: A Local Guide to Light, Timing, and Uncrowded Angles (2026)
Best photo spots in Hanoi
15 Best Photo Spots in Hanoi: A Local Guide to Light, Timing, and Uncrowded Angles (2026)
Discover the 15 best photo spots in Hanoi. Local timing tips, golden hour lighting windows, exact street coordinates, and uncrowded architectural angles.
Figure: Traveler walking along Long Bien Bridge pedestrian footpath in Hanoi at sunrise
Hanoi is one of Southeast Asia's most visually rewarding cities, but photographing it well requires patience and local understanding.
Between midday sun reflecting off white concrete, thousands of scooters parked on narrow pavements, and tangled bundles of overhead wiring, finding clean backgrounds can feel overwhelming. Many travelers end up with identical, crowded shots at the same three tourist landmarks.
To help you capture genuine, evocative photos of the capital, our team of local photo guides put together this curated list of
15 exceptional photography spots in Hanoi
.
We have organized them by neighborhood, with exact lighting recommendations, crowd avoidance tips, and composition notes so you know when and where to press the shutter.
Part 1: The Historic Old Quarter (Heritage & Street Life)
The 36 Guild Streets offer centuries-old texture: weathered ochre plaster, deep green French louvered shutters, and lively sidewalk commerce. The key here is early morning light before the delivery trucks arrive.
1. Hang Bac Street (The Silver Guild)
Best for: Classic Old Quarter architectural framing and heritage storefronts
Hang Bac is one of the oldest preserved streets in Hanoi, dating back to the 13th century when silver artisans migrated here to mint royal coin bars. The street is lined with narrow communal houses, gold-leaf shop signs, and vintage two-story facades.
Best Time:
6:45 AM – 8:00 AM.
Recommended Lens:
35mm or 50mm prime.
The Angle:
Stand on the northern side of the street near the intersection with Ta Hien, shooting down the curve of the road toward Dinh Kim Ngan (Silver Communal House). At 7:15 AM, morning sun cuts between the rooftops, creating dramatic shafts of golden light.
Pro Move:
Look for small family-run silver jewelry workshops where elderly jewelers sit behind glass display cases under tungsten desk lamps.
2. Ngo Huyen & Nha Chung (St. Joseph's Cathedral Alleyways)
Best for: European neo-Gothic texture combined with street cafes
While the front plaza of St. Joseph's Cathedral is usually packed with tour groups and selfie crowds, the perimeter alleyways—especially
Ngo Huyen
and
Au Trieu
—offer much calmer compositions.
Best Time:
7:30 AM – 8:30 AM or 4:30 PM (golden hour).
The Angle:
Walk down Ngo Huyen and shoot back toward the cathedral towers through the gap between modern cafes and ancient banyan trees. You capture the Gothic stone towers framed by vibrant green leaves and low coffee stools.
3. Hang Ma Street (Seasonal Colors & Paper Lanterns)
Best for: Rich background colors and seasonal market atmosphere
Hang Ma is Hanoi's traditional paper and ceremonial street. Depending on the month, it overflows with red silk lanterns, mid-autumn star lanterns, or festive ornaments.
Best Time:
8:00 AM – 9:00 AM (avoid evening crowds).
The Angle:
Position your subject walking slowly past the hanging lantern stalls. Use a wide aperture (f/1.8 to f/2.8) to blur the bustling background into a soft, glowing palette of red, gold, and magenta.
4. Dong Xuan Morning Market Perimeter (Cau Dong & Hang Khoai)
Best for: Raw documentary portraits and street texture
Inside the covered market, light is dim and chaotic. The photographic gold lies around the perimeter alleys—
Cau Dong
and
Hang Khoai
—where wholesale vegetable sellers and flower merchants trade off bicycle racks.
Best Time:
6:00 AM – 7:15 AM (the earlier, the better).
Related walking route:
Included in our Early Bird Sunrise & Local Markets Tour.
5. O Quan Chuong (Old East Gate)
Best for: Ancient brickwork and historical continuity
Built in 1749 and rebuilt in 1817, O Quan Chuong is the only intact city gate surviving from the ancient Thang Long citadel. Its arched brick passageway still carries daily pedestrian and bicycle traffic.
Best Time:
7:00 AM – 7:45 AM.
The Angle:
Frame your subject walking through the central brick archway, using the deep stone tunnel as a natural frame while morning sunlight illuminates the street beyond.
Part 2: The French Quarter (Colonial Charm & Grand Avenues)
Wide boulevards, neoclassical facades, and quiet tree-lined avenues define the area south of Hoan Kiem Lake. The visual language here is calm, elegant, and distinctly Indochinese.
Figure: Hanoi street vendor with vintage bicycle laden with fresh lotus flowers along yellow colonial wall
6. Sofitel Legend Metropole Perimeter (Ngo Quyen & Le Phung Hieu)
Best for: Timeless colonial architecture, white vintage cars, and wrought iron
Opened in 1901, the Metropole is Hanoi’s grand dame hotel. Its white-and-green exterior, classical awnings, and vintage Citroën cars parked on the perimeter provide an effortlessly sophisticated backdrop.
Best Time:
8:00 AM – 9:30 AM.
The Angle:
The corner of Le Phung Hieu and Ngo Quyen offers clean sidewalk lines, polished wooden louvered doors, and soft shaded light throughout the morning.
Related walking route:
Featured on our French Colonial Historical Footsteps Tour.
7. Hanoi Opera House Plaza (Nha Hat Lon)
Best for: Symmetrical grandeur and evening warm glow
Modeled after the Palais Garnier in Paris, this 1911 landmark sits prominently at the head of Trang Tien street with its pale yellow columns, slate roof, and broad stone steps.
Best Time:
7:00 AM – 8:00 AM (for empty steps) or 5:30 PM (blue hour when building floodlights switch on).
The Angle:
Shoot from the base of the wide stone steps looking up, or stand across the roundabout near the Hilton gardens using passing vintage Vespa scooters as foreground interest.
8. Trang Tien Walkway & Vintage Book Street
Best for: Nostalgic yellow colonnades and deep shadows
Trang Tien connects Hoan Kiem Lake directly to the Opera House. The north side of the street features covered sidewalk colonnades that create dramatic alternating bands of light and shadow on bright mornings.
Best Time:
8:30 AM – 10:00 AM.
The Angle:
Shoot down the covered pedestrian colonnade. The long vanishing line of pale yellow pillars and deep shaded ceilings naturally draws the viewer's eye straight toward your subject.
9. Cua Bac Church (Nha Tho Cua Bac)
Best for: Unique Art Deco & French-Vietnamese architectural synthesis
Located on Phan Dinh Phung street, Cua Bac Church was designed by French architect Ernest Hébrard in 1932. Unlike St. Joseph's European Gothic look, Cua Bac combines traditional Vietnamese curved roof tiles with Art Deco bell towers and ochre-yellow stucco.
Best Time:
8:00 AM – 9:30 AM.
The Angle:
The church courtyard is rarely crowded. Stand beneath the towering sưa trees and shoot upward toward the asymmetrical bell tower against a blue morning sky.
10. Phan Dinh Phung Street (The Golden Tree Canopy)
Best for: Dappled sunlight, leaf-covered sidewalks, and flower bicycles
Phan Dinh Phung is widely considered Hanoi’s most poetic avenue. Four rows of century-old Dracontomelon (
cây sấu
) trees create an uninterrupted green cathedral over the road.
Best Time:
7:30 AM – 9:00 AM (when morning rays pierce through the canopy).
Iconic Element:
Local women vendors pushing vintage bicycles laden with seasonal blossoms—lotus in summer, daisies in autumn, and white peach blossoms in spring.
Pro Move:
If you take a photo with a flower vendor, it is polite to purchase a bouquet (typically 50,000 to 80,000 VND / $2–$3) as a warm gesture of appreciation.
Part 3: Cultural, Waterside & Secret Viewpoints
Beyond the Old and French Quarters lie ancient lakeside causeways, historic railway bridges, and second-floor balconies that capture Hanoi from a completely different perspective.
11. Long Bien Bridge Pedestrian Footpath
Best for: Dramatic sunrise silhouettes, Red River mist, and historic iron trusses
Built by Daydé & Pillé between 1899 and 1902, this 2.4-kilometer cantilever steel bridge is a living museum. It survived multiple aerial bombings and remains in daily use by trains, motorbikes, and pedestrians.
Best Time:
5:30 AM – 6:45 AM (sunrise).
The Angle:
Walk roughly 300 meters along the pedestrian footpath starting from the Long Bien station ramp. Frame your subject walking along the wooden planks with the rusted steel trusses repeating toward the rising sun over the Red River.
Safety Note:
Motorbikes move quickly along the center track. Always remain within the dedicated wooden pedestrian walkway on the outer side.
12. Tran Quoc Pagoda Causeway (West Lake / Ho Tay)
Best for: Water reflections, lotus fragrance, and spiritual tranquility
Perched on a small island on West Lake, Tran Quoc Pagoda is the oldest Buddhist shrine in Hanoi, established in the 6th century. The causeway leading to the temple entrance is shaded by banyan trees and bordered by calm water.
Best Time:
6:30 AM – 7:30 AM or 5:00 PM sunset.
The Angle:
Stand on Thanh Nien street looking across the water toward the 11-story terracotta pagoda tower (
bảo tháp
). At sunset, the golden sky reflects directly off West Lake.
Related walking route:
Featured on our Spiritual & West Lake Breeze Tour.
13. Temple of Literature (Van Mieu - Quoc Tu Giam)
Best for: Ancient red lacquer pavilions, stone turtle stelae, and lotus ponds
Founded in 1070 as Vietnam's first national university, the complex consists of five serene courtyards. The traditional timber architecture, grey stone slabs, and manicured topiary trees provide an authentically Vietnamese heritage aesthetic.
Best Time:
8:00 AM sharp (doors open) before tour buses arrive at 9:00 AM.
The Angle:
The Khue Van Cac (Pavilion of the Constellation of Literature) framed over the Well of Heavenly Clarity (
Thien Quang Tinh
).
Dress Code:
Because this is a revered academic and Confucian shrine, shoulders and knees must be respectfully covered.
14. Phung Hung Street Railway Archways
Best for: Stone viaduct arches, urban murals, and vintage street lamps
Beneath the elevated train tracks running south from Long Bien station sits Phung Hung street. The 131 stone railway arches have been preserved, with several converted into public art murals celebrating old Hanoi street life.
Best Time:
8:00 AM – 9:30 AM.
The Angle:
Walk down the pedestrian promenade between Hang Cot and Hang Luoc. The massive granite blocks of the 120-year-old French viaduct offer clean geometric repeating arches for full-body portraits.
15. A Second-Floor Heritage Balcony Cafe (Old Quarter)
Best for: Intimate candid moments, egg coffee, and street-level vantage points
Some of Hanoi’s best photos are taken from above, looking down into the flow of bicycles, street vendors, and heritage roof tiles. Hidden cafes nestled on the second and third floors of French colonial apartments offer open wooden balconies.
Recommended Cafes:
Ban Cong Cafe
(Dinh Liet street),
Cafe Dinh
(second floor overlooking Hoan Kiem Lake), or
Loading T
(Chan Cam street).
Best Time:
8:30 AM – 10:00 AM.
The Angle:
Seat your subject at a small wooden table with a glass of warm egg coffee, shooting through hanging bougainvillea plants with the morning street scene softly blurred below.
Lighting Summary: When to Shoot in Hanoi
Table 1.1: When to shoot in Hanoi
3 Practical Street Photography Tips for Travelers
Travel Light (Ditch the Tripod):
Sidewalks in Hanoi are narrow and motorbikes weave through every alley. Setting up a three-legged tripod will slow you down, block pedestrian flow, and draw unnecessary attention. A fast prime lens (35mm or 50mm) on a lightweight camera body gives you all the speed and mobility you need.
Always Watch the Overhead Cables:
Hanoi's black utility cables are part of its street character, but a stray wire slicing across someone's face ruins an otherwise gorgeous portrait. Before pressing the shutter, take one second to check the top third of your frame and adjust your angle by taking two steps forward or crouching slightly.
Interact With Respect:
Street vendors and locals are generally welcoming, but always greet them with a polite smile (
"Xin chào"
) before pointing your camera directly at their face. If someone gestures no, lower your camera and move on with a nod of thanks.

Hiring a Private Photographer in Hanoi: Rates, Routes, and What to Expect (2026 Guide)
This guide outlines realistic rates for 2026, how a private session actually runs, the best street routes for natural light, and the practical details to check before booking.
Figure: Local photo guide and traveler walking through historic Old Quarter alley in Hanoi morning light
If you have spent even ten minutes scrolling through travel forums about Vietnam, you will notice a common dilemma: travelers love Hanoi's cinematic atmosphere, but getting decent photos of themselves here is surprisingly difficult.
Selfie sticks struggle with narrow alleyways and overhead power cables. Carrying a heavy tripod across cracked curbs and busy scooter traffic feels like a chore. And handing your smartphone to a well-meaning stranger usually results in cut-off feet, tilted horizons, or a rushed, blurry snap.
In recent years, booking a private walking photographer has become one of the most practical investments travelers make in Hanoi. It combines a relaxed neighborhood walk with a local companion who knows the light, understands the culture, and quietly captures documentary-style portraits while you explore.
This guide outlines realistic rates for 2026, how a private session actually runs, the best street routes for natural light, and the practical details to check before booking.
1. How a Private Photo Walk Actually Works
A private photo walk is fundamentally different from a studio session or a traditional wedding shoot. There are no portable reflectors, no costume racks, and nobody asking you to freeze in an unnatural pose for twenty seconds.
Instead, think of it as spending a calm morning with an English-speaking local friend who happens to carry a professional camera.
The Typical Morning Rhythm
Most sessions start early—typically between
7:00 AM and 8:00 AM
.
At this hour, the Old Quarter is just waking up. Street sweepers are finishing their rounds, women are setting out baskets of morning lotus flowers and herbs, and steam is rising from sidewalk noodle pots. The light is soft and angled low across the pale yellow French-colonial plaster.
During a 90- to 120-minute walk, you will cover roughly 1.5 to 2 kilometers at a relaxed pace. Your guide navigates through historic craft quarters, pauses in quiet residential courtyards, and stops for coffee at a hidden second-floor balcony.
7:00 AM — Meet guide at designated cafe or hotel lobby
7:15 AM — Walk through quiet craft streets (Hang Bac, Hang Be)
7:45 AM — Street portrait moments along textured colonial walls
8:15 AM — Break for traditional egg coffee at an open balcony
8:45 AM — Final candid portraits around Hoan Kiem Lake perimeter
9:00 AM — Review camera previews, wrap up session
Throughout the walk, the photographer gives simple, natural direction:
"Walk toward that archway,"
"Look over at that fruit vendor,"
or
"Take a sip of your coffee and look out over the street."
You stay focused on experiencing the city, while the photographer captures genuine, unforced moments.
Pro Move (Morning Light Window):
The direct sun turns harsh in Hanoi by 9:30 AM in the hotter months. If you want warm, flattering skin tones and empty street backgrounds, never start later than 8:00 AM.

3. The 4 Best Photography Neighborhoods in Hanoi
Hanoi is not a uniform city. Different quarters offer completely different textures, color palettes, and lighting conditions. Your photographer will usually recommend one of these four areas:
Figure: Traveler enjoying authentic egg coffee on French colonial balcony overlooking Hanoi Old Quarter
1. The Historic Old Quarter (Hoan Kiem)
Best for: Street culture, vintage architecture, dynamic lifestyle shots
The 36 Guild Streets represent the visual heartbeat of Hanoi. The architecture is characterized by "tube houses"—narrow street fronts with deep interiors, weathered mustard-yellow facades, and forest-green timber shutters.
Top photo spots:
Hang Bac (silver jewelry street), Hang Ma (lanterns and paper craft), and the narrow residential passageways off Hang Buom.
Recommended timing:
7:00 AM – 8:30 AM.
Related walking route:
Check our Early Bird Sunrise & Local Markets Tour.
2. The French Quarter (Trang Tien & Metropole Perimeter)
Best for: Elegant portraits, clean architectural lines, sophisticated European charm
South and east of Hoan Kiem Lake, the streets widen significantly. Here you will find grand neoclassical buildings, wide tree-lined sidewalks, wrought-iron balconies, and grand cream-colored facades.
Top photo spots:
The perimeter of the Sofitel Legend Metropole, Hanoi Opera House plaza, and Trang Tien book street.
Recommended timing:
8:00 AM – 9:30 AM or 4:00 PM – 5:30 PM.
Related walking route:
Explore our French Colonial Historical Footsteps Tour.
3. West Lake & Ancient Pagodas (Tay Ho & Ba Dinh)
Best for: Calm atmosphere, water reflections, traditional Vietnamese heritage
If you prefer open water, ancient banyan trees, and tranquil Buddhist architecture over energetic street markets, West Lake (
Hồ Tây
) is the natural choice.
Top photo spots:
Tran Quoc Pagoda causeway, the lotus ponds (in summer), and quiet lakeside residential paths near Tu Hoa street.
Recommended timing:
6:30 AM sunrise or 5:00 PM golden hour.
Related walking route:
See our Spiritual & West Lake Breeze Tour.
4. Long Bien Bridge & Morning Wholesale Markets
Best for: Raw industrial texture, gritty documentary portraits, dramatic morning skies

Santorini Park - A Lovely Photo Spot Right outside Hanoi
A blue-and-white photo studio park beside Yên Sở Park in southern Hanoi, built to look like Santorini — an unapologetically artificial, genuinely fun stop for a specific kind of photo.
I want to be upfront about what this place is, because I think a lot of write-ups dance around it: Santorini Park is not Santorini, it's not trying very hard to convince you it's Santorini, and it doesn't need to. It's a purpose-built photo studio in the Gamuda Land development, right by the Le Parc shopping center in Hoàng Mai district, a few steps from Yên Sở Park itself — whitewashed walls, blue domes, narrow stepped alleys, the whole Cycladic color palette laid over about 50,000 square meters of southern Hanoi. It exists specifically to be photographed, and once you accept that, it's a genuinely good time.
I went with a friend who was between wedding photo sessions — this is one of those places where you'll see actual couples in full bridal wear working through a shot list with a photographer and an assistant holding a reflector, alongside groups of teenagers in coordinated outfits doing the same thing with a phone on a tripod. There's no pretense of authenticity being punctured here; everyone knows what they came for.
What actually works, visually, is the density. The whole point of the real Santorini's photogenic quality is the way whitewashed buildings stack and curve against blue in tight, repeating patterns, and the designers here understood that instinct even if the materials are obviously newer and the scale is more compact. Certain corners — a blue staircase against a white wall, a bell-shaped dome against open sky — genuinely photograph well, better than I expected walking in skeptical. Other corners are more obviously thin, plywood-and-paint versions of the idea, and you'll notice the difference once you're looking for it.
Tickets run 80,000 VND for general entry, and the park is open from 7:30 AM to 7:00 PM, which gives you a decent window for both harsh midday light — good if you want strong shadows and saturated color — and softer late-afternoon light closer to closing, which flatters the white walls more. If you're planning a full shoot rather than a casual visit, there are wedding photo packages running around 450,000 VND that include more coordinated access, though for a casual visitor the general ticket is plenty.
Realistically, budget an hour, maybe ninety minutes if you're being thorough about getting shots at each backdrop, because the site isn't large enough to fill a whole afternoon on its own. Pair it with actual Yên Sở Park next door, which has real trees, a proper lake, and a much less curated kind of pleasant, for a fuller outing. Go on a weekday if your schedule allows it — weekend afternoons pull genuine crowds, mostly local groups doing coordinated outfit shoots, and you'll spend more time waiting for corners to clear than actually shooting.
It's not a place we'd usually build a whole session around, but if a client specifically wants that saturated, high-contrast blue-and-white look without booking a flight to Greece, it's a legitimate half-hour stop worth knowing about.

A local's guide to Hanoi's Old Quarter: a simple map, 10 things to do, a one-day plan, the weekend night market, where to stay and how to get there from the airport.
Hanoi's Old Quarter is the tight grid of streets just north of Hoan Kiem Lake. For centuries it was the city's merchant district, and it is still where most visitors sleep, eat and spend their first day. The first hour can feel like a lot: motorbikes, shopfronts spilling onto the pavement, smells of grilled pork and incense. Give it a morning and it turns into one of the most walkable neighborhoods in Asia.
This guide is written by Hanoi locals. It covers how the quarter is laid out, the things actually worth your time, a simple one-day plan, the weekend night market, where to stay, how to get here from the airport, and where to take the best photos.
Morning in the Old Quarter: a flower seller on her daily round.
Hanoi Old Quarter at a glance
Quick facts
Where
Hoan Kiem district, between Hoan Kiem Lake (south) and Dong Xuan Market (north)
Size
About 15 minutes' walk from the lake to Dong Xuan Market without stops
Best for
Street food, walking, small temples, shopping, people-watching
Best time of day
Early morning (quiet streets, soft light) and early evening (food stalls open)
Weekend extra
Walking street and night market, Friday to Sunday evenings
How long
One full day for the highlights, two to slow down
A simple mental map of the Old Quarter
Think of the Old Quarter as a rough triangle:
South:
Hoan Kiem Lake. The easiest landmark, and where most walks begin.
North:
Dong Xuan Market, the big covered market at the top of Hang Dao and Hang Ngang.
East:
the Long Bien Bridge approach and the dyke road along the Red River. O Quan Chuong, the old city gate, sits on this side.
West:
Phung Hung street and its brick railway arches.
Many streets still carry the name of the trade once practiced there.
Hang
means "goods": Hang Bac was silver, Hang Ma paper offerings, Hang Thiec tin, Hang Buom sails. A few streets still sell what their name promises, which is half the fun of walking here. Locals call the area "36 streets", although there are more than that today.
Map tip:
Save a few pins before you go: your hotel, Hoan Kiem Lake, Dong Xuan Market, St. Joseph's Cathedral and O Quan Chuong gate. Street names change at almost every corner, so an app with offline maps is more useful than a paper map. If you lose your bearings, walk until you reach the lake and start again.
10 best things to do in the Hanoi Old Quarter
1. Walk around Hoan Kiem Lake at sunrise
From first light, locals jog, dance and practice tai chi around the lake. Cross the red The Huc Bridge to Ngoc Son Temple before the tour groups arrive. Read more about
Ngoc Son Temple
.
2. Step inside a merchant's tube house at 87 Ma May
Old Quarter houses are narrow at the front and run deep into the block, with small courtyards to let in light and air. The restored heritage house at 87 Ma May shows how a merchant family lived and traded under one roof. Entry costs around 20,000 VND; check the current fee at the door.
3. Visit Bach Ma Temple
At 76 Hang Buom, Bach Ma ("White Horse") Temple is one of the oldest temples in the quarter. Legend says a white horse showed the king where to build the city walls. It is free to enter and usually opens in the morning and mid-afternoon, with a break at lunch. Dress modestly.
4. Find O Quan Chuong, the last old city gate
Thang Long once had several gates. O Quan Chuong, first built in 1749 and rebuilt in the early 1800s, is the only one still standing. Motorbikes still pass through it, which makes it a great spot to watch the city move.
5. Get lost in the small lanes
The main streets are busy, but narrow alleys open into courtyards, family shrines and tiny cafés. Start with our
5 Old Quarter alleys to slow down in
.
6. Drink egg coffee where it was invented
Egg coffee is a Hanoi original, whipped egg yolk and sugar over strong coffee. Read the story of
Café Giảng and how to photograph it
.
7. Explore Dong Xuan Market and Hang Ma street
Dong Xuan is the city's largest covered market and sells mostly wholesale goods: fabric, household items, dried foods. The food stalls around its edges are the real draw. Nearby, Hang Ma glows with paper lanterns and offerings, especially in the weeks before Mid-Autumn Festival and Lunar New Year.
8. See St. Joseph's Cathedral
The neo-Gothic
St. Joseph's Cathedral
stands on the quarter's southwest edge, with cafés and lemon-tea stalls on the steps around it.
9. Spend an evening on Ta Hien
Ta Hien and the streets around it fill with low plastic stools, cold beer and music after dark. Our guide:
Ta Hien street, where Hanoi nights come alive
.
10. Walk out to the railway and Long Bien Bridge
Hanoi's railway history runs along the quarter's edges. Read our
Train Street safety guide
before you go, and consider the calmer view from Long Bien Bridge at sunset.
The Huc Bridge and Ngoc Son Temple, best visited early before the tour groups.
One perfect day in the Old Quarter
Morning
6:00–7:30: Hoan Kiem Lake and The Huc Bridge while the city exercises.
7:30: Breakfast phở or bánh cuốn at a small shop with stools on the pavement.
8:30–11:00: 87 Ma May, Bach Ma Temple and the lanes around Hang Buom and Ma May.
Afternoon
Lunch: bún chả. See our
bún chả guide
.
Egg coffee break, then Dong Xuan Market and Hang Ma.
Late afternoon: O Quan Chuong gate, then walk toward Long Bien Bridge for sunset.
Evening
Chả cá on its own street, or street food around Dong Xuan.
Friday to Sunday: the walking street and night market. Any night: a beer on Ta Hien.
Want a slower version across two days? Try our
calm 48-hour Hanoi itinerary
.
Hanoi Old Quarter night market and walking street
From Friday evening to Sunday night, the streets around Hoan Kiem Lake close to traffic and become a walking street, with families, street games and live music.
Inside the Old Quarter, the weekend night market runs along Hang Dao, Hang Ngang and Hang Duong, heading north toward Dong Xuan Market. Expect clothing, souvenirs, snacks and crowds.
When:
Friday to Sunday, from around 7 pm until about midnight. Times can shift, so check with your hotel on the day.
Tips:
Go early in the evening before it gets packed. Keep your phone in a front pocket, and bargain politely at clothing stalls.
Where to eat in the Old Quarter
The Old Quarter is one of the best places in Vietnam to eat well on a small budget. Start with:
Bún chả:
grilled pork with noodles and herbs.
Our bún chả guide
.
Chả cá Lã Vọng:
turmeric fish with dill, a dish with its own street.
Origins and how to eat it
.
Bánh mì, phở and more:
see our
honest Hanoi street food guide
.
A simple rule: if a stall is full of locals and has one dish on the sign, order that dish.
Hanoi Old Quarter photos: where and when to shoot
Yellow facades, green shutters, tangled power lines, lanterns and shopfronts make the Old Quarter Hanoi's most photogenic neighborhood.
Early morning
for empty streets and soft light around the lake.
Late afternoon
for warm light on Hang Ma lanterns and the old gate.
Blue hour
for shop lights and motorbike trails, shot from the pavement or a café upstairs.
For exact spots and timing, see our
15 best photo spots in Hanoi
. Before you photograph people or shops, read our
Hanoi photography etiquette guide
.
Want photos of yourself in these streets, not just of the streets? See how a portrait looks around Dong Xuan in our
story of Thin with Harry
, or book a
private Hanoi photoshoot
with a local photographer-guide.
Thin outside Dong Xuan Market, photographed by Harry. The market sign keeps the Old Quarter in the frame.
Where to stay in or near the Old Quarter
Staying inside or on the edge of the Old Quarter puts you within walking distance of the lake, the food and the night market. Pick your area by how much noise you can live with.

Light sleepers should ask for a room away from the street. Curious about the French Quarter after dark? Our
Hanoi night photoshoot story
was shot around Trang Tien.
How to get from Hanoi airport to the Old Quarter
Noi Bai International Airport is roughly 30 km north of the Old Quarter. Allow 45–60 minutes by car, more at rush hour.
Ride-hailing (Grab, Xanh SM):
the simplest door-to-door option. Check the fare in the app before you confirm.
Airport bus 86:
leaves from outside the arrivals area and runs to Hanoi Railway Station, passing near the Old Quarter and Hoan Kiem Lake. It has a flat fare of about 45,000 VND and runs roughly every 30 minutes from early morning to around 10 pm. Check the current timetable before you fly.
City bus 17:
the cheapest option, to Long Bien bus station on the Old Quarter's edge. It is slower and makes more stops.
Hotel transfer:
many Old Quarter hotels arrange pickup. Confirm the price in writing.
Practical tips
Crossing the street:
walk at a steady pace and don't stop suddenly. Our
guide to crossing the street in Hanoi
explains how.
Pavements are parking lots.
Expect to walk in the road at times. Keep to the edge.
Dress for temples:
cover shoulders and knees for Ngoc Son, Bach Ma and other temples.
Cash helps:
many small food stalls prefer cash. Carry small notes.
Plan the bigger trip:
our
complete Hanoi travel guide
.
Frequently asked questions
How many days do you need in the Hanoi Old Quarter?
One full day covers the highlights. Two days let you slow down, add the French Quarter and enjoy more evenings.
Is the Hanoi Old Quarter safe?
It is generally safe for visitors, including solo travelers. The main risks are traffic and petty theft in crowds. Watch your phone and bag at night markets.
What is the best time of day to explore the Old Quarter?
Early morning, for quiet streets and soft light around the lake, and early evening, when the food stalls open.
Is the Old Quarter walkable?
Yes. Hoan Kiem Lake to Dong Xuan Market is about a 15-minute walk without stops, and most sights in this guide are within 20 minutes of each other on foot.
When is the Hanoi Old Quarter night market open?
Friday to Sunday evenings, from around 7 pm until about midnight, on Hang Dao, Hang Ngang and Hang Duong.
Is it better to stay in the Old Quarter or the French Quarter?
Stay in the Old Quarter for food and atmosphere on your doorstep. Choose the French Quarter if you want quieter nights and are happy to walk 10–15 minutes in.
Explore the Old Quarter with a local
The best way to see the quarter is on foot with someone who knows which alley leads to which courtyard. Our local hosts can turn your walk into photos you will keep.
